original_question: Let Diag be the class of Turing degrees d such that every ceer E != Id1 admits a d-computable diagonal function, where a ceer is a computably enumerable equivalence relation on ω and a diagonal function for E is a total function g with not(g(x) E x) for all x. How can the class Diag be characterized?
target_in_paper: Section 7 (Nikolay Bazhenov), Problem 25(i), the degree-theoretic problem of describing the class Diag for ceers with diagonal functions.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures Problem 25(i) almost exactly: it focuses on the class Diag of Turing degrees, stays within ceers on ω, includes the paper's exclusion E ≠ Id1, and uses the correct notion of a diagonal (fixed-point-free) function as a total function g with g(x) not E-equivalent to x for every x.
missing_details: If you keep the paper's notation E ≠ Id1, define Id1 explicitly; otherwise replace it by the stand-alone phrase 'E has more than one equivalence class.'
State the function type explicitly as a total d-computable map g: ω -> ω.
Make explicit that 'd-computable' means computable relative to an oracle of Turing degree d.
Define Diag with set-builder notation so the outer quantifier over Turing degrees is fully explicit.
To stay closest to the paper, use the official prompt 'Describe the class Diag' rather than the slightly looser wording 'How can the class Diag be characterized?'.
Keep the question confined to Problem 25(i), without merging in the separate reverse-mathematical and Weihrauch variants from Problem 25(ii)-(iii).
refined_question: Define Diag = { d : d is a Turing degree and, for every computably enumerable equivalence relation E on ω with more than one equivalence class, there exists a total d-computable function g: ω -> ω such that for every x in ω, g(x) is not E-equivalent to x }. Describe the class Diag.
justification: The draft matches the first version of Problem 25 in Section 7. The paper first introduces ceers and diagonal (fixed-point-free) functions, and then asks for a description of the degree class Diag. The refined version only makes the excluded trivial case explicit by replacing the paper's shorthand E ≠ Id1 with a stand-alone condition, and it intentionally does not drift into the separate reverse-mathematical or Weihrauch questions that appear immediately afterward. The nearby partial results that PA is contained in Diag, Diag is contained in DNR, and that some Martin-Löf random degree is not in Diag confirm that the intended scope is exactly the characterization of this degree class.
